title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarks & Runbooks (Team Wiki)
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This page is the canonical team wiki for the Serving Runtime: a consolidated reference covering runtime architecture, kernel scheduling strategies, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release highlights, common known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended for engineers on the serving-runtime, infra, and SRE teams who operate and evolve the inference runtime.

Goals
- Provide a single reference for architecture and scheduling rationale.
- Standardize profiling and benchmarking steps so performance work is reproducible.
- Document operational runbooks for common incidents and triage flows.
- Capture recent release notes and ongoing known issues to speed debugging.

Audience and ownership
- Primary audience: serving-runtime engineers, performance engineers, SREs.
- Owner: Serving Runtime team (primary), Eng-SRE (secondary).
- On-call escalation: see "Oncall and ownership" section.

1) Runtime architecture (high level)

Intro
The serving runtime is a horizontally distributed inference engine optimized for low-latency, high-throughput LLM inference on GPU fleets. Key design objectives: predictable latency (p50/p95/p99 SLOs), cost efficiency via batching and caching, and graceful degradation via routing and model fallbacks.

Core components
- Frontend / Ingress: authenticates requests, enforces quotas and rate limits, and fans requests into the dispatcher. (Service: runtime-ingress)
- Dispatcher: request coalescer and router. Implements routing policies (latency-first, cost-first, regional) and request admission. (Service: runtime-dispatcher)
- Scheduler / Kernel Selector: chooses execution kernels and schedules kernels onto GPU executors based on model profile, sequence length, and hardware topology. (Module: kernel-scheduler)
- Executor / Worker: GPU process responsible for executing kernels, managing KV cache and batching windows. (Service: runtime-executor)
- Cache Manager: maintains prefix/KV caches across requests and supports cache invalidation and TTL policies. (Module: kv-cache)
- Telemetry & Tracing: emits detailed traces, tensor-level metrics, and kernel timings to the observability stack. (Instrumentation: opentelemetry + custom exporters)

Data flow (short)
1. Ingress authenticates request and looks up route/model configuration.
2. Dispatcher groups compatible requests for batching and consults the kernel-scheduler.
3. Scheduler selects kernels and a scheduling plan (micro-batches, kernel sequence).
4. Executor runs kernels, updates KV cache, and streams tokens back to client.
5. Telemetry streams metrics: kernel_time_ms, queue_time_ms, batch_size, mem_alloc, tokens_out.

2) Kernel scheduling strategies and rationale

Design goals for scheduling:
- Match kernel choices to model architecture and sequence-length distribution.
- Minimize tail latency by isolating long sequences or heavy request types.
- Maximize GPU utilization without violating latency SLOs.

Primary strategies implemented:
- Per-model kernel profiles: each model has a profile (quantization, available kernels, optimal tile sizes). Kernel-selector uses the profile to prefer specialized kernels (e.g., fused attention vs generic matmul) when beneficial.
- Sequence-length bucketing: incoming requests are categorized into buckets (short/medium/long). Short buckets get prioritized micro-batching for low latency; long buckets are either routed to batch-only nodes or given isolated scheduling windows to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- Dynamic kernel switching: for a single session, the scheduler can switch kernels when the sequence length crosses thresholds (e.g., use memory-optimized kernels for very long contexts).
- Affinity & topology-aware placement: prefer executors on the same PCIe/NVLink island to reduce cross-device transfers for multi-GPU models.

Common kernel selection heuristics (pseudo):
- If model.quantized && request.length < 512 -> prefer quantized-fused-attn kernel.
- If request.is_streaming && p50_queue_time < 3ms -> use low-overhead dispatcher path.
- If batch_size >= profile.eff_batch_threshold -> enable grouped GEMM path.

3) Profiling playbook (how to profile an issue end-to-end)

Purpose
Reproducible procedure to collect traces and metrics when investigating performance regressions, kernel slowdowns, or tail latency spikes. Follow these steps before code changes that affect scheduling or kernel selection.

Pre-reqs
- Access to a test GPU cluster or dev GPU node.
- Profiling tools installed on executor images: nsight-systems, nvprof (deprecated but sometimes used), torch.profiler (if using PyTorch kernels), cupy/profiler for custom kernels.
- Feature flags: enable_profiling=true (per-node) to avoid noisy production traces.

Step-by-step
1. Reproduce workload: run the customer or synthetic workload on a staging fleet. Capture request logs with request-id.
2. Enable detailed tracing for the affected node: set exporter sampling to 100% for the short window.
3. Record an nsight-systems trace for the process (recommended). Example:
   sudo nsys profile --output /tmp/nsys_trace --trace=cuda,osrt --capture-range=process --duration 60s -- target-runtime-binary --args
4. Collect executor logs, kernel timings, and memory snapshots (dmesg and nvidia-smi --query).
5. Run flamegraph and kernel timeline analysis:
   - Convert nsys trace to timeline JSON and open in Nsight.
   - Extract kernel durations (per-kernel, per-stream).
6. If issue is scheduler-related, enable scheduler debug dump: /opt/runtime/bin/kernel-scheduler --dump-plan /tmp/plan.json while replaying requests.
7. For microbenchmarking kernels use the microbench suite (see Benchmarking suite section) to compare kernel variants with the exact model weights and input shapes.

Outputs to collect
- nsys trace file (.qdrep/.nsys-rep)
- scheduler plan dumps (JSON text)
- executor logs (stdout/stderr)
- telemetry metrics for the timeframe: kernel_time_ms, queue_time_ms, batch_size, gpu_util, mem_used_mb
- reproduction script (curl or loadgen config)

4) Benchmarking suite (standardized tests)

Overview
The benchmarking suite is used to measure throughput, latency and memory characteristics for models and kernel variants. All performance claims should come from results produced by this suite. Results are stored in the perf-bench DB and a canonical S3 bucket.

Benchmark types
- Token throughput (tokens/sec) at target batch sizes and concurrency.
- Latency P50/P95/P99 for single-request and streaming use cases.
- Memory footprint (peak GPU memory and per-layer allocations).
- Cold-start latency for fresh executors and warm KV-cache effects.
- Kernel microbench for GEMM, attention, and softmax primitives.

Canonical configs (table)
| test_name | model | sequence | batch_sizes | concurrency | notes |
|-----------|-------|----------|-------------|-------------|-------|
| smoke     | gpt-small | 64 | [1,4] | 2 | quick sanity check |
| latency-1 | gpt-medium | 128 | [1] | 1 | p99 latency baseline |
| throughput | gpt-large | 512 | [1,2,4,8] | 8 | saturated throughput |
| micro-kernel-gemm | n/a | varying | n/a | n/a | raw kernel timings |

How to run
- Use the bench orchestrator: benchctl run --config=bench-config.yaml --out=/results/<run-id>
- Each run must capture: benchctl metadata, model artifact id, git commit of serving runtime, node types used, and raw traces.
- Tag the run with labels (model, quantization, kernel-variant) so results are queryable.

Result storage and comparison
- Results are uploaded to s3://redwood-perf-bench/runs/<date>-<run-id>.
- Perf dashboard picks up results and computes deltas against last-green commit.
- Regression alerts: any run where p99 latency increases >10% or throughput drops >7% triggers the perf-alert workflow.

5) Release notes (recent highlights)

v2027.11.0 (released 2027-11-15)
- Introduced topology-aware scheduler optimizations for 8xA100 clusters. Expected p95 tail reduction of 12% for multi-GPU models.
- New quantized-fused-attn kernel (v3) available behind FF_quant_v3.
- Improved KV-cache eviction policy to reduce memory churn on long-context sessions.

v2028.01.10 (released 2028-01-10)
- Defaulted sequence-length bucketing thresholds for most production models (short=<128, medium=128-1024, long=>1024).
- Fixed a race in scheduler plan dumps that could cause corrupted plan.json files.
- Benchctl: added automatic artifacts tagging and perf run reproducibility checks.

Upgrade notes
- When upgrading to new kernel families, run the benchmarking suite on a representative set of models and workloads and hold traffic on a canary fleet for 24h before full rollout. See rollout checklist below.

6) Known issues (active and ongoing)

- Issue #4523: Intermittent p99 spikes for streaming requests on pods using fused-attn-v2. Workaround: enable slower-but-stable kernel fused-attn-v1 via model profile. (tracked, severity: medium)
- Issue #4688: Memory leak observed on GPU nodes when sequence length > 8k and KV-cache enabled. Temporary mitigation: enforce max_context_len=8192 on routes until fix lands. (tracked, severity: high)
- Issue #4801: On multi-tenant Dedicated clusters, preemption of low-priority nodes can sometimes cause model reloads that increase cold-start latency. Suggested: enable graceful-drain flag and set preemptible_life_seconds > 120.

7) Runtime runbooks (triage & mitigation)

A. High tail latency (p99) - runbook
1. Identify affected model/route via perf dashboard and metric tags (look for kernel_time_ms and queue_time_ms).
2. Check dispatcher queue depth and micro-batch sizes for the timeframe.
3. Run quick release controls: reduce max_batch_window_ms to 0 (force single-request path) for the affected model to confirm batching is contributing. CLI:
   curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" 
   https://console.redwood.internal/api/routes/<route>/config -d '{"max_batch_window_ms":0}'
4. If queue_time_ms is high and batch sizes are large, consider isolating long-context requests: apply sequence-length bucketing routing rule.
5. If kernel_time_ms dominates, collect an nsys trace for one executor for 60s and escalate to perf-engineering.
6. Postmortem: capture run id, scheduler dumps, and bench run comparisons.

B. OOM on an executor - runbook
1. Identify node(s) with OOM via team dashboard and kubernetes pod events.
2. Check model memory footprint from bench results and model.profile.
3. Mitigations (in order):
   a. Reduce per-pod concurrency (runtime-executor.max_concurrency).
   b. Reduce batch_size or enforce batch_size cap in model profile.
   c. Switch to memory-optimized kernel variant in model profile.
   d. If memory leak suspected, drain node and repro with --mem-trace enabled.
4. Collect executor core dump and related telemetry, open incident with tag "oom-executor".

C. Incorrect outputs / quality regression - runbook
1. Pin the serving version and compare outputs between versions using regression prompt-set from applied-ml-and-evals/prompt-sets-and-benchmarks.
2. If regression correlates to kernel change (quantization or fused kernels), rollback to previous kernel variant and notify model-onboarding.
3. Run a targeted eval suite and file a regression ticket with examples and diffs.

8) Release rollout checklist (canary->gradual)
- Create perf benchmark run for representative models (baseline).
- Deploy to canary fleet (5% traffic).
- Monitor p50/p95/p99 and error-rate for 24 hours. Thresholds: p99 <= baseline * 1.07, error_rate delta < 0.1%.
- If green, increase to 25% and monitor for 12 hours.
- If green, full rollout and follow-up bench run to confirm production measurements.
- After rollout, mark perf run with tag "release-<version>" and attach scheduler plan dumps.

9) Operational guidance & tooling
- benchctl: primary CLI for running benchmarks (repo: infra/perf-bench).
- telemetry dashboard: runtime/kernels view with drilling by model and node.
- perf-alerts: automated alerts on p99 regressions.
- scheduler debug flags: --dump-plan, --log-execution-path, --simulate-affinity

10) Team wiki links & references
- Model onboarding checklist: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding/model-onboarding-checklist
- Quantization profiles and guidance: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles
- Runbooks and incident history: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems

Appendix A - Example CLI snippets
- Run a smoke latency bench:
  benchctl run --config=bench-config.yaml --test latency-1 --out /tmp/run-$(date +%s)

- Collect an nsys trace on executor pid 12345:
  sudo nsys profile --output /tmp/trace-12345 --trace=cuda,osrt --target-pid 12345 --duration 60s

- Dump scheduler plan (debug only):
  curl -sS -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" 
    https://runtime.internal/api/scheduler/dump?node=<node-id> -o /tmp/plan.json

Appendix B - Contact and escalation
- Primary owners: serving-runtime@redwood.com (team alias)
- Perf engineering: perf-eng@redwood.com
- Oncall rotation: see team rota at /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/oncall-rota
- Pager escalation: PagerDuty service "Serving Runtime" (severity mappings: Sev1-prod, Sev2-stable, Sev3-info)

Appendix C - Playbook for kernel microbenchmarking
1. Pull exact production model artifact and weights: model-id from model-catalog.
2. Run micro-kernel harness with identical input shapes and dtype. Example: python microbench/gemm_bench.py --shape 2048 4096 --dtype fp16 --reps 1000
3. Compare kernels: baseline vs fused vs quantized. Keep experiment logs in /results and tag runs.

Document maintenance
- This page is maintained by the serving-runtime team. Major architecture changes, scheduler heuristics, or runbook edits require owner approval and reviewers. Update the "last_updated" field when content changes.
